extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, USPTO staff, patent practitioners, industry stakeholders (companies, inventors, investors)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how patent subject-matter eligibility jurisprudence affects patenting outcomes, investment, innovation, and technology sectors (e.g., AI, quantum, life sciences), and identifying standards the law should meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, predictable, and consistently applied eligibility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: “The standard for determining whether an invention is eligible for patenting should be clear, predictable, and consistently applied.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders repeatedly request clarity and consistent application across courts and the USPTO to reduce uncertainty. Lack of clarity forces applicants and examiners to guess which claims will survive, increasing prosecution and litigation costs and reducing reliable expectations for investors and innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid expansion of judicial exceptions that create uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics cautioned that the jurisprudence has “unreasonably and improperly expanded the scope and application of the judicially created exceptions to eligibility,” producing inconsistency, uncertainty, and unpredictability in issuance and enforcement of patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy evaluation should guard against broadening exceptions (e.g., abstract ideas, natural phenomena) in ways that sweep in traditionally patentable technologies. Examples cited include mechanical devices and diagnostics being treated as abstract/natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should provide meaningful exclusion of competitors (sufficient scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that do issue should provide meaningful exclusion of competitors in the market rather than being of narrow scope and uncertain value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders report that issued patents are sometimes narrow and may not exclude competitors effectively. Evaluations should consider whether claim scope is sufficient to incentivize investment and commercialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility should not force extraneous limitations into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants report needing to “add otherwise extraneous limitations to claims for the sole purpose of satisfying an undefined standard.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undefined or vague eligibility standards encourage claim-drafting anti-patterns—tacking on irrelevant technical details solely to survive eligibility scrutiny. Reform or guidance should reduce incentive for such workarounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility law should accommodate algorithm-based diagnostics and data-driven inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments noted that algorithms that process large datasets to produce diagnostic tests or personalized-medicine outputs can be novel, useful inventions, yet “under current patent eligibility jurisprudence, the very activity that produces a new, useful, and unobvious diagnostic test is not patent eligible because the process of diagnosis involves the execution of an algorithm.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should recognize when algorithmic/data-processing steps contribute a technical solution rather than being mere ineligible abstract ideas. Examples: bioinformatics used for treatment decisions, algorithms that process thousands of measurements to create diagnostic tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility rules should balance preventing overly broad/abusive patents and enabling innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters of current jurisprudence argued the new standard is a useful tool for addressing overly broad patents and defending against abusive suits by patent assertion entities (PAEs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A policy rubric should weigh the benefit of curbing abusive/overbroad claims (reducing litigation and PAE harm) against the risk of deterring valid, technically inventive claims. Consider both deterrence of abusive assertions and downstream investment effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability to support startups and SMEs (investment reliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many stakeholders—particularly innovators in life sciences—argued that unpredictability in eligibility “stifles innovation and hurts businesses, particularly startups and SMEs that are most dependent on outside sources of funding.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should include how eligibility uncertainty affects financing decisions of startups/SMEs and whether reliable patent rights are necessary to attract outside capital. Look for evidence of altered patenting/investment strategies among SMEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure impact on investment and innovation using empirical economic indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders urged evaluation of whether current subject-matter jurisprudence negatively impacts investment in innovation, citing metrics such as venture funding amounts, growth rates, and digital-economy GDP share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete metrics: VC funding totals and year-over-year changes, compound annual growth rates (CAGR) for patent applications/grants in affected technologies, GDP contribution of digital economy, and comparative international investment trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting trends (counts and growth rates) as evidence of sector health
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters pointed to increases in AI-related patent grants and patent-application growth in quantum and machine-learning areas as evidence that current jurisprudence has not harmed innovation in those sectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider studies and numbers (e.g., IEEE finding nearly fivefold more AI-related USPTO grants in 2018 vs 2008; cited CAGRs) when assessing whether eligibility jurisprudence correlates with declines or growth in patenting activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve public disclosure incentives (avoid driving innovators to trade secrecy)
rubrics_metrics.description: In diagnostics and precision medicine, some innovators stated they are no longer seeking patents and are turning to other forms of IP protection, such as trade secrets, at the cost of decreased disclosure of new technological information to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy assessment should consider whether eligibility rules incentivize private disclosure (patents) or secrecy, and the resulting effects on public access to technical information and follow-on innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-neutral application of eligibility (avoid special rules by sector)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many commenters argued the same reasoning should apply to AI and emerging technologies as to past disruptive technologies; patents have adapted historically (e.g., software, genetic engineering) without special carve-outs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymaking and examiner guidance should aim for technology-neutral principles that do not grant special extra patentability or restrictiveness based solely on the technology label (AI, quantum, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-makers should be informed about specific technologies before judging impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters advised the USPTO, judiciary, and other decisionmakers to take time to learn about technologies (e.g., quantum computing) before determining the impacts of current jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include stakeholder engagement, technical education, and domain-specific inquiry when forming eligibility guidance or adjudicating cases to avoid misclassification (e.g., treating quantum effects as mere natural phenomena without context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating routine software/AI steps as patent-eligible without technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Some argued AI software inventions are more likely to be directed toward abstract ideas under Alice and subsequent case law than other software inventions, suggesting careful scrutiny of purported technical contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility analysis should focus on whether claimed software/AI steps add a technical solution or are routine/abstract data manipulation. Anti-patterns include granting patents for high-level functional descriptions lacking technical implementation detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess national competitiveness effects of eligibility jurisprudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters claimed that eligibility jurisprudence affects the United States’ position relative to foreign competitors in leadership of critical, emerging technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating eligibility policy, include measures of international competitiveness: comparative patenting activity, investment flows (e.g., AI deals by country), and industry leadership indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat eligibility as both legal and factual question where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit / Supreme Court debate referenced whether eligibility (e.g., ‘directed to’ an abstract idea) is a question of law or a question of fact, affecting how predictable and reviewable determinations are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and procedural guidance should clarify what aspects of eligibility are legal (de novo review) versus fact-based (benefit of trial factfinding), since this influences reviewability, precedent stability, and predictability for applicants.
